questions.stem: Which of these is not one of the three steps of divide and conquer?
options: divide the problem into smaller problems of the same kind
questions.explanation: Comparing every pair is what O(n2) sorts do; divide and conquer is exactly the way to avoid it.

questions.stem: The recurrence for the number of steps of merge sort on n elements is:
questions.explanation: Two sorts of half the size, plus a merge that touches all n. (a) is binary search; (c) is quicksort's worst case; (d) would be a divide and conquer whose combine step is O(1).

questions.stem: _merge merges two sorted runs of 4 elements each. The largest number of comparisons it can make is:
questions.explanation: Each comparison sends one element to scratch, and the last element needs none: at most 4 + 4 - 1 = 7, when the two runs interleave to the end (for example [1, 3, 5, 7] and [2, 4, 6, 8]).

questions.stem: Merge sort is stable because:
options: it splits the array exactly in the middle
on a tie, _merge takes the element from the left run
questions.explanation: The <= in if a[i] <= a[j]. With < the sort is still correct but no longer stable (W10-B1). Where it splits (a) has nothing to do with it.

questions.stem: The extra space merge sort needs, beyond the input, is:
questions.explanation: One scratch Array of n slots, shared by every merge, plus an O(log n) call stack — O(n) in total.

questions.stem: How many calls of _merge does merge_sort make on 8 elements?
questions.explanation: Every merge joins two runs into one; starting from 8 runs of one element, 7 merges leave one run. In general n - 1.

questions.stem: merge_sort(list(range(1024))) — already sorted — makes how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: On sorted input each merge of two runs of m elements empties the left run after m comparisons: n/2 log2 n = 512 × 10 = 5{,}120 (measured). 523,776 (d) is quicksort with pivot="first"; 1,023 (a) is Timsort.

questions.stem: During Lomuto's partition, with j the next index to look at, the invariant is:
questions.explanation: The smaller-than-pivot values sit in a[lo:boundary], the others in a[boundary:j]; a[j:hi] is still unknown, so (d) claims too much.

questions.stem: _partition(a, 0, 7) on a = [6, 3, 9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 4] returns:
questions.explanation: The pivot is 4; only 3, 1 and 2 are smaller, so it lands at index 3: [3, 1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 7, 6].

questions.stem: How many comparisons with the pivot does one Lomuto partition of a range of 8 elements make?
questions.explanation: One comparison per non-pivot element, n - 1 = 7, whatever the order.

questions.stem: quick_sort(list(range(n)), pivot="first") makes:
questions.explanation: Every pivot is the smallest of its range, so each partition peels off one element: (n-1) + (n-2) + … + 1. For n = 1,024 that is 523,776 comparisons, measured.

questions.stem: On an already sorted range, pivot="median3" avoids the worst case because:
options: the median of the first, middle and last values is the middle value, which splits the range in half
questions.explanation: Of the first, middle and last values of a sorted range, the middle one is the median — the exact middle of the range. Median-of-three does cost comparisons (a), and it is not random (b).

questions.stem: Quicksort recurses into the smaller part and loops on the larger. This bounds:
options: the call stack at O(log n) frames
the running time at O(n log n)
the number of swaps at n
the stack at O(1) on every input
questions.explanation: Each recursive call is on at most half of its caller's range, so there are at most log2 n frames. The time is still O(n2) in the worst case (b). On sorted input with "first" the stack is O(1), but not on every input (d).

questions.stem: Quicksort is not stable because:
options: its partition swaps elements across long distances
it may use a random pivot
questions.explanation: A swap in the partition can move an element past its equal, and nothing puts them back. Recursion (a) and in-place work do not by themselves break stability.

questions.stem: In the array layout of a heap, the children of index i are at:
questions.explanation: With the root at index 0. (b) is the layout with the root at index 1, used in some textbooks.

questions.stem: Build-heap on [4, 10, 3, 5, 1, 8, 2, 7] gives:
questions.explanation: The sifts at indices 3, 2, 1, 0 give [4, 10, 3, 7, 1, 8, 2, 5], [4, 10, 8, 7, 1, 3, 2, 5], unchanged, and [10, 7, 8, 5, 1, 3, 2, 4] (W10-T4). A heap is not sorted (a, b).

questions.stem: Build-heap is O(n), not O(n log n), because:
options: most nodes are near the bottom, where a sift-down is short
the input is already a heap
questions.explanation: About n/4 nodes can sink 1 level, n/8 can sink 2, … — the sum n(1/4 + 2/8 + 3/16 + …) is at most n. Measured: about 1.9 n comparisons, the same ratio from n = 1,000 to 8,000.

questions.stem: For n = 10, heap sort's build loop sifts down the indices:
questions.explanation: From the last parent, n // 2 - 1 = 4, down to 0. Indices 5 to 9 are leaves. Going up (d) is W10-B2's bug.

questions.stem: Which sort is O(n log n) in the worst case and needs only O(1) extra space?
questions.explanation: Merge sort (a) needs O(n) extra; quicksort (c) is O(n2) in the worst case; insertion sort (d) is O(n2).

questions.stem: The lower bound of about n log2 n comparisons applies to:
questions.explanation: The argument counts yes/no answers to comparisons. Counting sort (d) never compares and runs in O(n + k).

questions.stem: Python's sorted() and list.sort() use:
questions.explanation: Timsort, by Tim Peters (2002): natural runs, insertion sort on short runs, stable merging. Introsort (c) is C++'s std::sort.

questions.stem: sorted(list(range(1000))) — already sorted — makes how many comparisons?
questions.explanation: Timsort finds one ascending run of 1,000 in 999 comparisons and has nothing to merge (measured: 999).

essays.stem: Describe merge sort as divide and conquer. Write its recurrence and solve it with a recursion tree. Give its extra space, and explain what makes it stable.
essays.answer:
• Divide: split a[lo:hi] at mid = (lo + hi) // 2 — no comparisons. Conquer: sort both halves recursively; a range of 0 or 1 elements is sorted (base case). Combine: merge the two sorted runs with _merge.
  • Recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + cn, T(1) = c.
  • Recursion tree: the root merges n elements; its two children n/2 each; the four grandchildren n/4 each — every level totals n. The sizes halve, so there are log2 n levels that merge: T(n) = O(n log n), in every case, because the split never depends on the values.
  • Space: one scratch Array of n slots, plus log2 n stack frames: O(n). Not in place.
  • Stable: on a tie, _merge takes from the left run (<=), and the left run holds the elements that came first in the input.

essays.stem: Describe Lomuto's partition: what it does, its invariant, and why the pivot is in its final place afterwards. Why is there nothing to "combine" in quicksort?
essays.answer:
• Lomuto's partition takes the pivot a[hi] and one scan j = lo..hi-1. Values smaller than the pivot are swapped to the front, into a[boundary], and boundary grows. A final swap puts the pivot at a[boundary]; it returns boundary.
  • Invariant: a[lo:boundary] < pivot <= a[boundary:j]. True at the start (both empty), kept by each step, and at the end j = hi, so every value is on the correct side.
  • Final place: every value smaller than the pivot is to its left, every other value to its right; sorting either side cannot move any value across, so the pivot's position is its position in the sorted array.
  • No combine: after both parts are sorted, left part, pivot, right part is already in order — the partition did the combining in advance. Merge sort is the mirror image: free divide, expensive combine.

essays.stem: Compare the pivot strategies "first", "random" and "median3": the cost of choosing, and the inputs on which each is at its worst. Why is sorted input the case that matters?
essays.answer:
• "first" and "last": O(1) to choose. Worst on sorted and reverse-sorted input: the pivot is the extreme of its range every time, one element per level, n(n-1)/2 comparisons.
  • "random": O(1) plus a random number. No fixed input is bad for it: the worst case needs bad luck at almost every level, which is vanishingly unlikely; the expected cost is about 1.39 n log2 n.
  • "median3": up to three extra comparisons per partition. Exact middle on sorted and reversed input. Its worst case exists — specially built "median-of-three killer" inputs (Musser, 1997) — but it is not an input that occurs by accident.
  • Why sorted input matters: it is the most common input a real sort sees — data sorted before, with a few changes. A pivot rule that is worst on sorted input is worst exactly when it matters.

essays.stem: Explain how heap sort uses an array as a tree. Describe build-heap and the sort phase, and argue that build-heap is O(n). Why is heap sort often slower in practice than quicksort, though its worst case is better?
essays.answer:
• Array as tree: a[0] is the root; the children of a[i] are a[2i + 1] and a[2i + 2]; the parent is a[(i - 1) // 2]. The tree is complete, height ⌊ log2 n ⌋; there are no pointers.
  • Build-heap: sift down every parent from n // 2 - 1 down to 0; each sift may assume both subtrees are already heaps. Sort: swap the root (the max) with a[end], shrink the heap to a[0:end], sift the new root down; repeat for end = n - 1 … 1. O(n log n).
  • Build-heap is O(n): a node at height h sinks at most h levels, and there are at most n/2h+1 such nodes: Σh h  n/2h+1 ≤ n. Most nodes are leaves or near them.
  • Slower in practice: the sift jumps from i to 2i + 1 — far apart in memory, so caches help little — and it makes more comparisons (measured on random data: about 1.7 n log₂ n, against about 1.2 for median-of-three quicksort). Its strength is the guarantee: O(n log n) worst case with O(1) extra space.

essays.stem: Define a stable sort. Give a practical reason to want one, say which of the six sorts in dsa/sorting.py are stable, and explain why sorting (key, tag) tuples does not test stability.
essays.answer:
• Stable: elements with equal keys come out in the order they went in.
  • Why: sorting records by one field after another. Sort students by name, then stably by grade: within a grade they stay in name order.
  • In dsa/sorting.py: bubble, insertion and merge sort are stable; selection, quick and heap sort are not.
  • Tuples do not test it: Python compares (key, tag) tuples by the tag when the keys are equal, so every correct sort — stable or not — puts (1, "a") before (1, "c"). A stability test needs values that compare by key only, such as a class whose comparison methods look at the key alone.
